Chi-Squared Goodness of Fit

Background

In my Chi-Squared test of independence I asked whether two variables (car color and manufacturer) were related. A Chi-Squared goodness of fit test answers a different kind of question: does a single categorical variable follow some expected distribution? Using the same Belarus 2019 used-car dataset from Kaggle, we ask whether car colors are spread evenly across the palette, or whether buyers and manufacturers clearly favor some colors over others.

Hypothesis

If every color were equally common, each of the 12 colors would account for 1/12 of the cars. The goodness of fit test compares the observed color counts against that uniform expectation.

\[ H_0: \text{Car colors are uniformly distributed (each color equally likely)} \] \[ H_a: \text{At least one color occurs more or less often than a uniform distribution predicts} \] \[ \alpha = 0.05 \]

Analysis

The table and bar chart below show the observed count of each car color across the full dataset.

Table continues below
black blue brown green grey orange other red silver violet
7705 5802 886 2760 3751 184 2688 2925 6852 463
white yellow
4212 303

The distribution is visibly lopsided: black, silver, and blue dominate the market while orange, violet, and yellow are rare. We test whether that imbalance is statistically significant by comparing the observed counts to equal expected counts (each color = total / 12).

Chi-squared test for given probabilities: color_counts
Test statistic df P value
22609 11 0 * * *

The test returns a p-value far below our significance level of α = 0.05, so we reject the null hypothesis. Car colors are clearly not uniformly distributed.

To see which colors drive that result, we examine the Pearson residuals. Large positive residuals mark colors that appear far more often than a uniform distribution would predict.

Table continues below
black silver blue white grey red green other brown
79.31 64.26 45.73 17.67 9.531 -5.046 -7.958 -9.228 -41.03
violet yellow orange
-48.49 -51.32 -53.42

Black and silver carry the largest positive residuals, confirming they are the most over-represented colors relative to an even split, while the vivid colors sit well below expectation.

Interpretation

The used-car market in this data has strong color preferences rather than an even spread. Neutral, resale-friendly colors like black, silver, blue, grey, and white dominate, while bold colors like orange, violet, and yellow are scarce. Because the goodness of fit test produced a p-value far below α = 0.05, we reject the null hypothesis and conclude that car colors do not follow a uniform distribution. This complements my Chi-Squared independence analysis: not only is color related to manufacturer, but the overall color palette itself is heavily skewed toward conservative choices.

Credit/References

This analysis is modeled after my other portfolio analyses and used mild AI assistance for plotting.

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(mosaic)
library(ggthemes)
library(pander)

data <- read.csv("C://Users/Alex/Documents/GitHub/Portfolio/AB_TESTS/cars.csv")
```

## Background

In my Chi-Squared test of independence I asked whether two variables (car color and manufacturer) were related. A Chi-Squared goodness of fit test answers a different kind of question: does a single categorical variable follow some expected distribution? Using the same Belarus 2019 used-car dataset from Kaggle, we ask whether car colors are spread evenly across the palette, or whether buyers and manufacturers clearly favor some colors over others.

## Hypothesis

If every color were equally common, each of the 12 colors would account for 1/12 of the cars. The goodness of fit test compares the observed color counts against that uniform expectation.

$$
H_0: \text{Car colors are uniformly distributed (each color equally likely)}
$$
$$
H_a: \text{At least one color occurs more or less often than a uniform distribution predicts}
$$
$$
\alpha = 0.05
$$

## Analysis

The table and bar chart below show the observed count of each car color across the full dataset.

```{r}
color_counts <- table(data$color)
pander(color_counts)
```

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
ggplot(data, aes(x = fct_infreq(color), fill = color)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Car Color",
       y = "Count",
       title = "Car colors are far from evenly distributed") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

The distribution is visibly lopsided: black, silver, and blue dominate the market while orange, violet, and yellow are rare. We test whether that imbalance is statistically significant by comparing the observed counts to equal expected counts (each color = total / 12).

```{r}
gof <- chisq.test(color_counts)
pander(gof)
```

The test returns a p-value far below our significance level of α = 0.05, so we reject the null hypothesis. Car colors are clearly not uniformly distributed.

To see which colors drive that result, we examine the Pearson residuals. Large positive residuals mark colors that appear far more often than a uniform distribution would predict.

```{r}
pander(sort(gof$residuals, decreasing = TRUE))
```

Black and silver carry the largest positive residuals, confirming they are the most over-represented colors relative to an even split, while the vivid colors sit well below expectation.

## Interpretation

The used-car market in this data has strong color preferences rather than an even spread. Neutral, resale-friendly colors like black, silver, blue, grey, and white dominate, while bold colors like orange, violet, and yellow are scarce. Because the goodness of fit test produced a p-value far below α = 0.05, we reject the null hypothesis and conclude that car colors do not follow a uniform distribution. This complements my Chi-Squared independence analysis: not only is color related to manufacturer, but the overall color palette itself is heavily skewed toward conservative choices.
